file.path: /mnt/data/J of Risk   Insurance - 2025 - Bergesio - Optimal insurance design under limited liability.pdf

metadata.title: Optimal insurance design under limited liability

raw_text.abstract: We study optimal demand for insurance in a classical expected utility setting where the insured party has limited liability and has access to three different types of progressively more restrictive contracts. At one end, with no restrictions on the indemnity schedule, it is optimal to fully insure certain losses while leaving others uninsured. At the other end, if indemnity schedules and retained losses are assumed to be increasing functions of the underlying loss, the optimal insurance policies are shown to be capped deductibles. For the intermediate case when the indemnity schedule is only an increasing function of the loss, we find that optimal contracts exhibit a richer structure beyond the capped policies suggested in earlier literature. Our study extends and provides a unifying perspective on the existing literature on optimal insurance under limited liability.
raw_text.keywords_text: expected utility, insurance, limited liability, optimal demand

theoretical_summary: In an expected-utility model with limited liability, optimal insurance contracts depend on contract-shape restrictions, ranging from selective full insurance to capped deductibles and richer increasing-indemnity structures.

metadata.title: Wildfire risk and municipal bond yields

raw_text.abstract: Wildfires increased in frequency and severity over the past 30 years, raising the exposure of municipalities. We study whether municipal bond yields reflect wildfire risk and find that the municipal bond market begins pricing wildfire risk around 2000. A one‐standard‐deviation rise in wildfire risk leads to a 3.646 basis points increase in a bond's yield spread, increasing financing cost for affected communities. The effect on yield spreads disappears for maturities of less than 1 year or more than 15 years, supporting the view that wildfire risk is a medium‐term risk. When including measures of investor attention into our analysis, we find that investor attention is associated with an additional increase in yield spreads. Fire mitigation measures, on the other hand, are associated with a reduction in yield spreads, highlighting the benefits of wildfire risk management for municipal financing.

metadata.title: Gambling for market recovery? European insurers' corporate bond investments during market stress

raw_text.abstract: Using daily stock market data for European insurers, I investigate how a stock market contraction, as experienced during the COVID‐19 pandemic, affects insurers' credit risk allocation of their corporate bond portfolio. I find that insurers shift their portfolio holdings pro‐cyclically towards lower credit risk assets in the first month of the market contraction. As the crisis progresses, I find evidence for counter‐cyclical, riskier investment behavior by European insurers, especially in high‐yield instruments, that can neither be explained by credit rating downgrades of held bonds nor by hedging with CDS derivatives. This counter‐cyclical investment behavior cannot be observed for US firms, which provides evidence for a difference in investment behavior between US and European insurers. The observed investment behavior of European insurers could be beneficial for systemic stability by attenuating price declines through insurance liquidity provision, but excessive risk‐taking by insurance companies over longer periods can also reinforce systemic stress.

metadata.title: Extreme-weather risk and the cross-section of stock returns

raw_text.abstract: We document an extreme‐weather risk premium in the cross‐section of stock returns. Between 1995 and 2019, stocks of domestic U.S. firms with the most negative sensitivity to aggregate storm losses earned an annual excess‐return spread of more than 6 percentage points relative to those with the most positive sensitivity, a difference not explained by standard factors. Fama‐MacBeth regressions confirm that more negative storm‐risk betas predict higher subsequent returns. The premium concentrates in geographically exposed and historically affected firms and in institutionally held stocks, consistent with fundamental‐risk and salience channels. Our results establish a link between physical climate risk, the cost of equity, and ultimately firm value.

metadata.title: Pollution liability insurance and corporate environmental compliance in China

raw_text.abstract: This study examines the effect of a pollution liability insurance mandate on corporate environmental compliance in Shenzhen, China. We employ a triple differences design, comparing electroplating and circuit board (ECB) manufacturing firms, mandated to purchase insurance, to industries and a neighboring city without the mandate. Results show a 0.48 reduction in annual environmental violations per firm (a 72% decrease) across all Shenzhen ECB firms. Within the Shenzhen ECB industry, only about half of firms comply. Notably, both insured and uninsured firms reduced violations, consistent with anticipation that (eventual) premiums would depend on past violations. The insurance could generate two opposing forces: premium‐based incentives to reduce violations versus moral hazard among the insured. We find suggestive evidence that insured firms' environmental compliance gains are partially offset by moral hazard. Our findings demonstrate that premium‐based incentives dominate and effectively counteract market failures due to asymmetric information, increasing environmental compliance on net.

metadata.title: Cyber risk assessment for capital management

raw_text.abstract: This paper introduces a two‐pillar cyber risk management framework to address the pervasive challenges in managing cyber risk. The first pillar, cyber risk assessment, combines insurance frequency‐severity models with cybersecurity cascade models to capture the unique nature of cyber risk. The second pillar, cyber capital management, facilitates informed allocation of capital for a balanced cyber risk management strategy, including cybersecurity investments, insurance coverage, and reserves. A case study, based on historical cyber incident data and realistic assumptions, demonstrates the necessity of comprehensive cost–benefit analysis for budget‐constrained companies with competing objectives in cyber risk management. In addition, sensitivity analysis highlights the dependence of the optimal strategy on factors such as the price of cybersecurity controls and their effectiveness. The framework's implementation across a diverse range of companies yields general insights on cyber risk management.

theoretical_summary: A two-pillar framework integrates a cyber cascade loss model with a capital-allocation problem to jointly optimize cybersecurity investment, insurance coverage, and reserves under budget constraints.

file.path: /mnt/data/J of Risk   Insurance - 2025 - Côté - A fair price to pay  Exploiting causal graphs for fairness in insurance.pdf

metadata.title: A fair price to pay: Exploiting causal graphs for fairness in insurance

raw_text.abstract: In many jurisdictions, insurance companies are prohibited from discriminating based on certain policyholder characteristics. Exclusion of prohibited variables from models prevents direct discrimination, but fails to address proxy discrimination, a phenomenon especially prevalent when powerful predictive algorithms are fed with an abundance of acceptable covariates. The lack of formal definition for key fairness concepts, in particular indirect discrimination, hinders effective fairness assessment. We review causal inference notions and introduce a causal graph tailored for fairness in insurance. Exploiting these, we discuss potential sources of bias, formally define direct and indirect discrimination, and study the theoretical properties of fairness methodologies. A novel categorization of fair methodologies into five families (best-estimate, unaware, aware, hyperaware, and corrective) is constructed based on their expected fairness properties. A comprehensive pedagogical example illustrates the implications of our findings: the interplay between our fair score families, group fairness criteria, and discrimination.
raw_text.keywords_text: bias, causal inference, directed acyclic graph, discrimination, disparate impact, fairness criteria, score

theoretical_summary: A causal-graph framework for insurance pricing formalizes direct and indirect discrimination and classifies fairness methods into five score families with distinct expected fairness properties.

metadata.title: Registered index-linked annuities in qualified retirement plans

raw_text.abstract: Many Americans remain financially underprepared for retirement. While automatic enrollment in employer-sponsored retirement plans has helped, target-date funds (TDFs) used as default investments have limitations. We propose target-date registered index-linked annuities (TD-RILAs) as a transparent, cost-effective alternative providing decreasing equity exposure over time. A theoretical analysis explores TD-RILAs' optimal structure and compares them to TDFs. A lab experiment examines investors' preferences, product transparency, default choices, and the role of information. We find that TD-RILAs are a suitable addition to retirement plans, potentially rivaling TDFs.

metadata.title: Shared exposures or management fashions? Antecedents of convergence in the insurance and banking industries

raw_text.abstract: We study convergence in the attention of decision-makers across the insurance and banking industries. Our analysis is based on textual risk disclosures (10-K reports, 2006–2018), providing a snapshot of corporate priorities and contexts. We theoretically link convergence with decision-making contexts via the Attention-Based View. Leveraging strategic management theory, we identify antecedents of convergence in attention and, therefore, potentially, risk contagion. These include common trends in the macro-environment, substitution threats, and management fashions. We combine this theoretical framework with machine learning tools to create quantitative measures of convergence in attention and its antecedents. We find that the proposed measure of convergence is predictive of inter- and intra-industry stock correlations. Finally, based on regression and sensitivity analyses, we identify the relative importance of different antecedents, showing that shared risk management fashions largely drive inter-industry convergence in attention. This highlights challenges when interpreting regulatory text data in the context of predicting contagion risk.

metadata.title: Spatio-temporal risk sharing and transfer: A unified theory of multi-period decentralized insurances and annuities

raw_text.abstract: Two distinct strands of research focus on decentralized risk sharing plans. One strand centers on classic risk sharing and decentralized insurance, including peer-to-peer insurance, mutual aid, and DeFi insurance. The other explores decentralized annuities, such as tontine and group self-annuitization. Despite their disparate development paths, both involve decentralized risk sharing and transfer among participants. This paper aims to unify these domains by extending a theory of decentralized insurance to encompass multi-period decentralized insurances and decentralized annuities. The framework illuminates connections between spatial risk sharing and intertemporal risk transfer, and enables economic analysis of diverse scheme designs. The paper also provides a comprehensive review of various notions of temporal and spatial actuarial fairness, elucidating how different designs emerge from these distinct notions.

metadata.title: Basis risk, social comparison, perceptions of fairness, and demand for insurance: A field experiment in Ethiopia

raw_text.abstract: Index insurance lowers agricultural risk but covers only covariate risks. Since farmers do not have complete insurance, they may develop mistrust of insurance when experiencing crop losses and not receiving payouts. Although recent innovations in remote sensing enable the provision of more complete insurance including coverage for idiosyncratic risks, such insurance introduces differences in payouts within social networks, which might be considered unfair, introduce jealousy, and depress insurance demand. We conduct a lab‐in‐the‐field experiment with farmers in Ethiopia to examine whether providing complete insurance coverage affects perceived fairness and insurance demand. We also examine effects of informing farmers about neighbors' payout experiences. We find that such social comparison increases perceived fairness of index insurance. Providing complete crop insurance increases perceived fairness of outcomes and willingness to pay for insurance, without introducing jealousy over neighbors receiving different payouts. These results are concentrated among men and those with little insurance knowledge.

metadata.title: Regulating risk culture in the insurance industry using machine learning

raw_text.abstract: This study examines the relationship between risk culture and regulation in the insurance industry using textual analysis and machine learning. By analyzing 10‐K disclosures, we classify firms into distinct risk culture clusters and find that the risk culture of insurance firms is significantly shaped by their uncertain risk strategies, constraints in defining, implementing, and reporting risks, as well as litigious decisions and risk management practices. metadata.title: Housing wealth and long‐term care insurance demand: Survey evidence

raw_text.abstract: This paper uses survey methods to assess the impact of access to housing wealth on long‐term care (LTC) insurance demand. We compare two new mechanisms to finance LTC insurance with housing wealth: reverse mortgage loans and home reversion (partial sale and leaseback). Using data from an online survey of urban Chinese homeowners, we find that housing liquidity increases the stated demand for LTC insurance. On average, the survey participants spent 15.7% of their given total wealth to buy LTC insurance when they could use savings and a reverse mortgage, 12.8% when they could use savings and home reversion, and 5.2% when they could only use savings. Product demand was linked to economic factors, demographic variables, health, bequest motives, house price expectations, product understanding, and financial capability. Our results inform the design of new public or private sector programs that allow individuals to access their housing wealth while ‘aging in place’.

metadata.title: Market discipline in life insurance: Does public risk disclosure encourage less risky management actions?

raw_text.abstract: We analyze how public risk disclosure, specifically Solvency II, impacts life insurers' risk‐taking behavior. Using data from 58 German life insurers from 2016 to 2023, we find that publicly reported solvency ratios can affect premium growth and surrender rates. Moreover, insurers appear to improve their solvency ratios following a decline in the previous year. To investigate whether policyholder behavior drives a life insurer's reduced risk‐taking, we then develop a model in which a life insurer seeks to maximize shareholder value. Unlike previous research, we consider annually disclosed solvency ratios, affecting policyholders' dynamic purchase and surrender behavior. In our model, the insurer acts less riskily (e.g., holds more reserves and sells less‐risky insurance portfolios) to maintain higher solvency ratios and mitigate policyholders' adverse reactions. Our findings motivate public risk disclosure to strengthen market discipline, but its level and design must be carefully calibrated to be effective and avoid undue costs.

metadata.title: Welfare consequences of the compound risks of index insurance

raw_text.abstract: Index insurance is an attractive variant on the standard insurance contract that allows the determination of a loss event to be defined by one or more thresholds on an index that is positively correlated with actual losses. Index insurance also comes with a compound risk, basis risk. We examine how these compound risks for index insurance affect behavior towards the decision to purchase the product or not. Using incentivized experiments, we control the actuarial specifics of contracts offered, the information provided to decision makers, and our knowledge of the risk preferences of decision makers. We demonstrate that individuals that fail to process compound risks, end up purchasing the contract more than other individuals, as well as more than they should, generating significant welfare losses. We also develop a natural information treatment that mitigates these welfare losses.

metadata.title: Heterogeneity in health insurance choice: An experimental investigation of consumer choice and feature preferences

raw_text.abstract: We investigate heterogeneity in health insurance choice using data from a controlled laboratory experiment. Participants make consecutive choices from sets of insurance plans that vary in premium, deductible, and complementary coverage of illnesses. We find that there is considerable heterogeneity in how much individuals are willing to pay for certain plan attributes. To better understand these differences, we account for individual risk preferences using a rank‐dependent expected utility (RDEU) model and assess the welfare effects of plan choices. At the aggregate level, we find welfare losses under both the normative RDEU model and the descriptive EV model. At the individual level, however, the results are more differentiated: for some individuals, choices are consistent with their RDEU preferences, whereas for others, choices do not fit either model, suggesting either decision errors or reliance on heuristics.

raw_text.abstract: We examine an optimal portfolio problem where an individual receives nontraded labor income and must decide how to allocate her wealth between a stock and a risk‐free asset, while also determining the optimal time to retire. metadata.title: Catastrophe risk sharing among individuals, private insurance, and government

raw_text.abstract: Limited research has been conducted on the optimal public–private risk‐sharing for catastrophe risks. This paper develops a theoretical framework to study the risk‐sharing decisions and interactions of three types of catastrophe‐market participants: a large number of individuals, a large number of private insurers in a competitive market, and a government that can choose between alternatives of re/insurance or ex post relief. Our analysis shows that the optimal government intervention varies depending on the correlation levels among individual losses. For moderately positive levels of loss correlation, it is optimal for the government to offer an ex post relief program to supplement private insurance. However, for higher levels of loss correlation, government reinsurance becomes optimal, although not to the extent of replacing private insurance if the government is less efficient than private firms. In sum, as catastrophe‐loss correlations increase, that is, as the risk becomes more catastrophic, more risk‐sharing tools and funding are needed to maximize social welfare.

theoretical_summary: A social-planner and market-equilibrium framework with individuals, competitive insurers, and a taxing government shows that optimal public intervention shifts from ex post relief to government reinsurance as loss correlation rises, with private insurance generally remaining part of the efficient risk-sharing mix when government operations are less efficient.

file.path: /mnt/data/J of Risk   Insurance - 2024 - Abdikerimova - Multiperiod peer‐to‐peer risk sharing.pdf

metadata.title: Multiperiod peer-to-peer risk sharing

raw_text.abstract: Risk sharing has been practiced in various forms in the financial industry. This paper is the first to study both dynamic and static risk-sharing mechanisms for a group of participants over multiple periods. The design of risk-sharing strategies is based on the Pareto optimization of quadratic utilities of participants' reserves. Building on the most common form of reinsurance—pro rata treaties, we propose a peer-to-peer (P2P) network for risk sharing. Assuming independent multivariate losses over time, we find that the optimal risk-sharing allocation exhibits a three-component structure with the long-term limit and two correction terms. This allows us to show convergence of the risk-sharing solution and the ratios of long-term reserves. Furthermore, we study the impact of actuarial fairness on various risk-sharing strategies and their long-term limits.
raw_text.keywords_text: financial fairness; mean–variance objective; multiperiod optimization; peer-to-peer network; risk management; risk sharing

sections.introduction: Motivates multiperiod peer-to-peer (P2P) risk sharing as an extension of classic risk-sharing and portfolio selection, emphasizing temporal smoothing and long-run behavior of allocations and reserve ratios under proportional sharing.
sections.method: Formulates dynamic and static proportional P2P allocation problems with market-clearing constraints and a social-planner objective based on quadratic utilities of terminal reserves; derives closed-form optimal allocation matrices with a long-run recipient-indifferent component plus correction terms; studies actuarial fairness constraints and variants.
sections.results: Shows the optimal dynamic allocation decomposes into (i) a recipient-indifferent long-run allocation determined by second-moment weights and (ii) correction terms driven by expected terminal reserves and current reserve imbalances; proves convergence of allocations and reserve ratios under time-homogeneous losses; characterizes how actuarial fairness alters limits and weights.
sections.conclusion: Concludes that multiperiod P2P risk sharing yields tractable closed-form solutions with convergence to recipient-indifferent allocations, providing theoretical justification for pro-rata style sharing and a foundation for extensions (e.g., nonproportional sharing and added cash flows).

theoretical_summary: The paper derives closed-form optimal proportional peer-to-peer risk-sharing rules over multiple periods under Pareto optimization of quadratic utilities, showing a three-part allocation structure and convergence to recipient-indifferent long-run allocations under time-homogeneous losses with extensions under actuarial fairness.

file.path: /mnt/data/J of Risk   Insurance - 2024 - Alexander - The market for model laws  The diffusion of NAIC model laws.pdf

metadata.title: The market for model laws: The diffusion of NAIC model laws

raw_text.abstract: The National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC) issues model laws to promote uniformity in the US state-based insurance regulatory system. In this paper, we study the diffusion of 197 NAIC model laws, examining the adoption patterns and influencing factors. Employing a network algorithm, we uncover the underlying network over which model laws spread. The NAIC plays a central role in this network, and its influence increases over time. Additionally, we explore factors affecting states' model law adoptions from three perspectives: the laws' attributes, the states' internal characteristics, and external influences. We find that a law's attributes play a key role. Model laws characterized by low complexity, distinct from existing state laws, mandated for accreditation compliance, and recently amended are more likely to be adopted. While we do not find significant impacts of various state-internal characteristics, our results reveal that states follow geographic and ideological neighbors in adopting model laws.
raw_text.keywords_text: insurance regulation; NAIC model laws; policy diffusion network

sections.introduction: Frames NAIC model laws as a policy-diffusion process in U.S. state-based insurance regulation and asks (i) what the general diffusion pattern is (NAIC versus early-adopting states as leaders) and (ii) how law attributes, state internal traits, and external peer influences shape adoption decisions.
sections.data: Compiles model-law adoption status across states from NAIC sources for 197 existing model laws and tracks amendment histories; augments with NAIC meeting proceedings (committee membership and motivations), insurance department resources reports (staffing, budgets, complaints/inquiries), commissioner tenure, and state political/economic covariates; constructs a law–state–year panel (baseline 1960–2017; subset 1998–2017 when department variables are available).
sections.method: Infers a persistent diffusion network of leaders and followers from repeated adoption timing using a latent diffusion-network algorithm (NetInf) treating the NAIC as a node alongside states; then models state-year adoption decisions in a law–state–year panel using discrete-time adoption probability models with fixed effects and covariates capturing law complexity and novelty, accreditation relevance, amendment recency, prior similar state laws, and geographic/ideological peer adoption exposure.
sections.results: Finds the NAIC is the central node in the inferred diffusion network with rising influence over time, while some states act as subcenters; in adoption determinants, law attributes dominate—lower complexity, greater distinctness from existing state laws, accreditation relevance, and recent amendments increase adoption likelihood—while most state-internal characteristics have weak explanatory power; identifies peer effects via geographic and ideological neighbors and additional boosts for widely adopted laws with federal motivation and commissioner committee involvement.
sections.conclusion: Concludes that NAIC-led diffusion and policy design features of model laws are the primary drivers of cross-state adoption, implying that clarity, perceived advantage, and accreditation/federal linkages matter more than broad state resource differences for regulatory uniformity.

empirical_analysis.measuring_method_Y: Law–state–year adoption indicator coded as 1 if a state has enacted the current or a previous version of an NAIC model law (treating ‘current version’ and ‘previous version’ as adoption actions) and 0 otherwise, based on NAIC adoption tables and related records.
empirical_analysis.measuring_method_X: Model-law characteristics constructed from NAIC documents, including text complexity proxies (e.g., count of defined terms and readability indices), amendment recency defined as 1/(adoption-year minus latest-amendment-year plus 1) with 0 if none, accreditation-program membership indicator, and ‘state fatigue’ measured as the count of prior adoptions of similar state laws before a given year; supplemented by external-peer exposure measures (neighbor adoption shares and ideological distance) as described in the paper.
empirical_analysis.methodology: Two-stage empirical design: (i) infer a leader–follower diffusion network from adoption timing across repeated binary adoption cascades (including NAIC as a network node) and (ii) estimate state adoption probabilities in a law–state–year panel using a discrete-time adoption model with state and year fixed effects and covariates for law attributes, state internal characteristics, and external peer influences.
empirical_analysis.Robustness check method: Alternative definitions of ‘neighbors’ (border-sharing versus NAIC zone), alternative sample start-of-risk definitions (e.g., earliest adoption year versus NAIC adoption year), and subsample analyses incorporating insurance-department resource variables when available; additional specifications varying included department variables to address collinearity concerns, as described in the paper.
empirical_analysis.dataset_and_period: Law–state–year panel covering NAIC model laws and U.S. states, baseline 1960–2017; extended data from NAIC model-law texts and histories, NAIC meeting proceedings, and state-level political/economic covariates; subset 1998–2017 adds state insurance department and market variables where available.
empirical_analysis.control_variables: State political and socioeconomic controls (e.g., divided government, ideology index, legislative professionalism, population, per-capita income), insurance department and market measures (e.g., commissioner tenure, department budget and staffing, complaints/inquiries, P/C and L/H premium volumes), plus state and year fixed effects as described in the paper.
subject: Identify how NAIC model laws diffuse across U.S. states and quantify how model-law design features and peer influences shape the likelihood and timing of state adoption in a state-based insurance regulatory system.

file.path: /mnt/data/J of Risk   Insurance - 2024 - Apicella - A behavioral gap in survival beliefs.pdf

metadata.title: A behavioral gap in survival beliefs

raw_text.abstract: Life span uncertainty (longevity risk) impacts several economic decisions. Individuals can form and revise their survival beliefs making use of behavioral heuristics. We propose a model of sentiment, in which individuals are assumed to switch between optimistic and pessimistic expectations of their health. When optimism is persistent in the face of health shocks, or when individuals are more likely to change their sentiment from pessimistic to optimistic than otherwise, our model predicts survival underestimation at young ages and overestimation at old ages. An empirical analysis based on the longitudinal data from Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe validates our model.
raw_text.keywords_text: longevity risk; mortality risk; sentiment; subjective beliefs

sections.introduction: Motivates systematic gaps between subjective and actuarial survival probabilities and proposes a sentiment-switching behavioral mechanism to explain underestimation of survival at younger ages and overestimation at older ages, with implications for retirement-related financial decisions.
sections.data: Uses longitudinal microdata from SHARE (Waves 2 and 4–8) for adults aged 50+ in Austria, Belgium, Denmark, France, Italy, Sweden, and Switzerland; constructs subjective survival probabilities, sentiment proxies, health-status measures (self-rated health and diagnosed conditions), and actuarial benchmarks built from national mortality data with sentiment- and health-class adjustments.
sections.method: Constructs actuarial survival probabilities by forecasting baseline mortality with a two-factor stochastic mortality model on national mortality data and then adjusting death rates for sentiment class and health-status classes estimated from SHARE period-study mortality experience; relates changes in subjective survival beliefs to sentiment upgrades/downgrades and health shocks while comparing updates against the adjusted actuarial benchmarks.
sections.results: Finds sentiment is strongly associated with subjective survival belief updates; subjective beliefs underreact to severe health shocks relative to actuarial updates; and the age-patterned gap persists even when actuarial benchmarks incorporate sentiment and health status, indicating a behavioral component beyond private information.
sections.conclusion: Concludes that sentiment-driven optimism/pessimism contributes to systematic survival-belief biases and suggests implications for product design and communication in longevity-related insurance and retirement planning.

empirical_analysis.measuring_method_Y: Survey-elicited subjective survival probability (0–100 scale) answering the percent chance of living to a target age (target age depends on current age in the SHARE expectations module); analyzed in levels and changes between consecutive waves.
empirical_analysis.measuring_method_X: Survey-based optimism proxy ‘Good Future’ from SHARE (“How often do you feel that the future looks good for you?”) coded 1–4 (never/rarely/sometimes/often), including indicators for upgrades/downgrades between waves and sentiment-class grouping for mortality adjustments.
empirical_analysis.methodology: Longitudinal analysis linking belief updates to sentiment switching and health shocks while benchmarking against actuarial survival probabilities constructed by forecasting national mortality and adjusting death rates for sentiment and health-status classes estimated from observed mortality experience in SHARE.
empirical_analysis.Robustness check method: Sensitivity analyses excluding focal-point survival answers (0%, 50%, 100%) across waves and alternative mortality-adjustment parameterizations and health-shock definitions as described in the appendices.
empirical_analysis.dataset_and_period: SHARE Waves 2 and 4–8 (older adults 50+) in seven European countries; actuarial benchmarking uses national mortality data and a SHARE-based period study over 2011–2017 to estimate sentiment- and health-class mortality adjustments.
empirical_analysis.control_variables: Age and age-squared; gender; country; change in forecasting horizon; functional limitations; counts of diagnosed diseases by severity; changes in self-assessed health and life satisfaction; socioeconomic changes (income, net worth, expenditure categories) and other demographic status changes as described in the paper.
subject: Test whether optimism–pessimism sentiment switching explains systematic biases in subjective survival beliefs relative to actuarial benchmarks that incorporate respondents’ sentiment and health status, and quantify how belief updates respond to health shocks across ages.

file.path: /mnt/data/J of Risk   Insurance - 2024 - Bello - Annuity puzzle  Evidence from a Swiss pension fund.pdf

metadata.title: Annuity puzzle: Evidence from a Swiss pension fund

raw_text.abstract: We analyze individual annuitization decisions at retirement in an environment with mandatory participation in a funded pension pillar and low average annuity price. Using administrative data from a large Swiss insurance company over the period 2011–2015, we document that, even in this favorable environment, only 42.7% of the retirees fully annuitize, against 45% taking full lump sum. We show that individual annuitization decisions strongly respond to financial incentives, measured by the Money Worth Ratio, and to the tax rates on annuity and lump-sum payments. Lump-sum payments are more common among French- and Italian-speaking individuals. Using Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe data, we show that French- and Italian-speaking Swiss are more likely to leave inheritance—thus suggesting that preferences for bequests may affect annuitization decisions. Finally, we provide evidence of asymmetric information, using the unused observable test, to show that individuals living in high mortality municipalities are less likely to annuitize and more likely to cash out their pension wealth.
raw_text.keywords_text: annuity demand; culture; mortality risk; passive adverse selection

sections.introduction: Studies the annuitization choice at retirement in Switzerland’s mandatory second-pillar system where annuity conversion rates are administratively set at favorable levels, and asks why substantial lump-sum take-up persists despite low annuity prices.
sections.data: Administrative contract-level retirement payout choices from a large Swiss insurer (second pillar) for 2011–2015 (about 12–13k retirees), linked to canton/municipality tax schedules and municipal mortality statistics; complementary SHARE survey data for Swiss respondents to proxy bequest-related attitudes and related preferences across language groups.
sections.method: Constructs individual annuitization outcomes (full annuity, annuity share, full lump sum), calculates Money Worth Ratio (MWR) as expected present value of annuity payments divided by pension wealth using national mortality tables and an alternative MWR using municipal mortality via a fitted Gompertz hazard; computes individual average tax rates for annuity versus lump sum by municipality and canton; tests cultural effects using the language of insurer statements; tests asymmetric information using the unused observables approach by relating municipal mortality rates to annuitization choices.
sections.results: Finds sizeable under-annuitization even in a favorable pricing environment; annuitization increases with higher MWR and with higher lump-sum taxation and decreases with higher annuity taxation; French/Italian-language statement recipients are less likely to annuitize and more likely to prefer lump sums; higher municipal mortality predicts lower annuitization consistent with passive adverse selection; SHARE evidence suggests Latin-language Swiss have stronger bequest intentions that plausibly mediate the cultural pattern.
sections.conclusion: Concludes that annuitization reflects a mix of financial incentives, taxes, culture-linked bequest motives, and passive adverse selection via information not used in pricing, implying policy levers through pricing/taxes and improved communication of longevity risk and product flexibility.

empirical_analysis.measuring_method_Y: Three retirement payout outcomes from insurer records: (i) full annuity indicator equal to 1 if annuity share equals total pension wealth, (ii) annuity_share defined as annuitized pension wealth divided by total pension wealth, and (iii) full_lump_sum indicator equal to 1 if annuity share equals 0.
empirical_analysis.measuring_method_X: Money Worth Ratio (MWR) defined as the expected present discounted value of the promised annuity payment stream divided by initial pension wealth using survival probabilities from Swiss mortality tables and a discount rate aligned with the technical rate; alternative MWR uses municipality-specific survival probabilities derived by fitting a Gompertz mortality curve to municipal death and population data and mapping to individual age/sex/municipality.
empirical_analysis.methodology: Retirement-choice analysis combining insurer administrative data with constructed annuity valuation (MWR) and individualized tax-rate measures; evaluates how valuation and fiscal incentives, cultural proxies, and unused mortality information correlate with the annuitization decision in a mandatory-participation environment.
empirical_analysis.Robustness check method: Alternative discrete-choice specifications for binary outcomes; alternative discount-rate assumptions in MWR construction; alternative spouse-income assumptions for joint taxation to recompute tax rates; specifications including additional local socioeconomic controls and alternative mortality-based MWR definitions.
empirical_analysis.dataset_and_period: Administrative Swiss second-pillar payout records from a large insurer for retirements 2011–2015, linked to federal/cantonal/municipal tax schedules and Swiss mortality data (national and municipal); complementary SHARE Switzerland waves (2004–2017) used to compare bequest intentions and related preferences across language groups.
empirical_analysis.control_variables: Pension wealth level and squared (and interactions with gender); conversion rate applicable to annuitization; average tax rate on annuity income and on lump-sum payout computed at municipality/canton; canton and year fixed effects; gender; municipal characteristics (average income, share foreigners, share upper-secondary education) in selected specifications.
subject: Explain why retirees under-annuitize even when annuities are favorably priced by quantifying how annuity valuation, taxes, culture-linked bequest preferences, and local mortality information predict annuitization choices in Switzerland’s mandatory second-pillar system.

file.path: /mnt/data/J of Risk   Insurance - 2024 - Berry‐Stölzle - Insurers  climate change risk management quality and natural disasters.pdf

metadata.title: Insurers' climate change risk management quality and natural disasters

raw_text.abstract: We perform a textual analysis of insurers' climate risk disclosures and construct a climate change risk management quality index. Our index captures to what extent insurers identify, manage, and adjust their business model to climate change risk. We find that natural disasters in an insurer's home state lead to an increase in climate change risk management quality. The effect of natural disasters in an insurer's geographic markets on climate change risk management seems to be less pronounced. Overall, these results are consistent with salience theories of choice.
raw_text.keywords_text: climate risk; disclosure; insurance; sentiment analysis; textual analysis

sections.introduction: Examines heterogeneity in insurers’ climate-risk management and tests whether salient local climate-related events (natural disasters near headquarters) spur improvements in disclosed climate-risk management quality beyond information contained in disaster activity across the firm’s underwriting markets.
sections.data: NAIC Climate Risk Disclosure Survey filings (2012–2020) merged with statutory financial statements; natural-disaster measures from EM-DAT aggregated to state-year and adjusted by subtracting historical state averages; state macro controls (GDP and unemployment) linked to insurer headquarters state; final panel includes thousands of insurer-year observations across U.S. insurers.
sections.method: Constructs an RMQuality index from disclosure text using preprocessing, a risk-management-quality bigram dictionary seeded from regulatory guidance and expanded via keyword discovery, and sentence-level scoring that accounts for negation; relates RMQuality to adjusted disaster counts in the home state and in underwriting markets with firm and year fixed effects and controls, interpreting home-state shocks as salience after conditioning on market disasters.
sections.results: Finds that unexpectedly high disaster activity in the insurer’s home state is associated with higher RMQuality, while disaster activity in geographic underwriting markets is weaker or insignificant once home-state disasters are included; effects are strongest for property–liability insurers and for publicly traded firms with governance pressure; improved RMQuality predicts better subsequent performance proxies in lagged analyses.
sections.conclusion: Concludes that salient local disasters induce insurers to invest more in climate-risk management as reflected in disclosure quality, consistent with salience-driven attention, with implications for regulators seeking timely improvements in insurers’ climate preparedness.

empirical_analysis.measuring_method_Y: Text-based climate risk management quality index (RMQuality) computed from NAIC Climate Risk Disclosure Survey narrative responses by counting and sentiment-adjusting occurrences of a context-specific bigram dictionary (seeded from New York DFS climate-risk guidance, expanded via keyword discovery) and averaging standardized per-sentence scores to obtain an insurer-year RMQuality.
empirical_analysis.measuring_method_X: Adjusted annual number of natural disasters in the insurer’s headquarters state (#NatDisHQ), constructed from EM-DAT by counting state-year disasters and subtracting the state’s historical mean over 1900–2011 to isolate the unexpected component; parallel measures for underwriting markets include premium-weighted adjusted disaster counts across all states where the insurer writes business (#NatDisMarket) and a dominant-market variant (#NatDisMIMarket).
empirical_analysis.methodology: Panel analysis of insurer-year RMQuality as a function of unexpected natural-disaster activity in the headquarters state and in underwriting markets, using firm and year fixed effects and standard insurer and state controls to isolate the incremental salience effect of local disasters.
empirical_analysis.Robustness check method: Alternative disaster measures using extreme events and specific hazard types; disaster severity using total damages and insured damages instead of counts; alternative RMQuality constructions and sample restrictions excluding insurers concentrated in their home state; subsample analyses by business type and organizational form; governance analyses incorporating public-trading and blockholder indicators.
empirical_analysis.dataset_and_period: U.S. insurer-year panel from NAIC Climate Risk Disclosure Survey filings matched to statutory financial statements for 2012–2020; natural-disaster data from EM-DAT for U.S. events (2012 onward) with historical baselines from 1900–2011; state macro data from BEA (GDP) and BLS (unemployment).
empirical_analysis.control_variables: Insurer size (log assets); profitability (ROE/ROA measures as defined); capital-to-assets ratio; reinsurance usage (ceded premium share); voluntary disclosure indicator; mutual/group indicators; home-state mandatory-disclosure indicator; headquarters-state real GDP and unemployment; product and geographic diversification measures in business-type subsamples.
subject: Assess whether salient natural disasters near insurer headquarters spur measurable improvements in climate-risk management quality as reflected in mandated climate-risk disclosures, beyond information from disaster activity in the insurer’s underwriting markets.

file.path: /mnt/data/J of Risk   Insurance - 2024 - Biener - More options  more problems  Lost in the health insurance maze.pdf

metadata.title: More options, more problems? Lost in the health insurance maze

raw_text.abstract: While the opportunity to choose from a diverse range of options can be advantageous, consumers often struggle to make optimal decisions in the domain of health insurance. In this study, we examine the effects of decision aids on improving choice optimality in a health insurance setting that allows for variations in coverage but is standardized otherwise. While this relatively simplistic setting theoretically implies optimal conditions for observing large fractions of optimal choices, we observe widespread adoption of non-welfare-maximizing plans, with at least 36% of the population winding up with suboptimal insurance plans. In a hypothetical-choice survey experimental setting, we estimate the treatment effects of increasing transparency through information provision and restricting choice on choice optimality. We find that decision quality cannot be improved meaningfully by our interventions and that nonoptimal choice is economically relevant, as it accounts for an increase of approximately 9.4% in total annual cost.
raw_text.keywords_text: health insurance; policy; value of choice

sections.introduction: Evaluates whether simplifying choice menus or adding transparent consequence information improves consumers’ deductible-plan choices in the Swiss mandatory health insurance market, where coverage is standardized and deductible choice is the primary margin of contract variation.
sections.data: Laboratory-based hypothetical choice experiment with randomized treatment arms conducted at the University of St. Gallen (2019 and 2020) using a student subject pool, paired with Swiss Federal Office of Public Health and Federal Statistical Office inputs to parameterize premiums and objective health-cost distributions for plan optimality benchmarks.
sections.method: Defines normative optimal deductible choice using expected-utility calculations under regulated Swiss pricing and risk-type proxies; randomizes participants into conditions that vary presentation (standard text vs consequence graphs) and information (adding probabilities, simplifying probabilities, capping cost range) and a restricted menu with only boundary deductibles; measures plan-choice optimality and expected financial loss relative to the optimal deductible using objective and belief-based risk distributions.
sections.results: Finds substantial selection of nonoptimal intermediate deductibles in both market data and the experiment; consequence-graph displays increase selection of normatively sensible boundary plans but do not materially reduce expected financial losses; restricting choice raises selection of the cost-efficient high deductible for the low-risk subject pool but can increase large mistakes for some, leaving average loss reductions modest and statistically weak; probability-information add-ons do not shift subjective beliefs, limiting effectiveness.
sections.conclusion: Concludes that nonoptimal deductible menus generate economically meaningful welfare losses that are not easily corrected by information provision or menu restriction alone, motivating policy designs such as age-based defaults, fewer middle options, or redesigned premium discounts aligned with risk.

empirical_analysis.measuring_method_Y: Plan-choice optimality measured as (i) indicator for choosing one of the two normatively sensible boundary deductibles (CHF 300 or CHF 2500) and (ii) expected annual financial loss in CHF defined as the difference in total costs borne by the insured between the objectively cost-efficient deductible (CHF 2500 for the low-risk lab population) and the selected plan, computed using population health-cost distributions and the regulated Swiss premium schedule.
empirical_analysis.measuring_method_X: Random assignment to information and menu treatments: consequence-graph presentation of mapping from incurred health costs to out-of-pocket spending; variants adding conditional probability information or simplified probability summaries; visual cap on displayed health-cost range; and a restricted menu offering only the CHF 300 and CHF 2500 deductibles.
empirical_analysis.methodology: Randomized hypothetical-choice laboratory experiment evaluating how information presentation and choice-set restriction affect deductible-plan selection and welfare loss in a standardized Swiss health-insurance environment.
empirical_analysis.Robustness check method: Alternative definitions of optimality using subjective belief distributions as private information; heterogeneity analyses by subjective cost beliefs (optimistic vs pessimistic) and participant attributes; specifications controlling for demographics and numeracy; comparisons across Swiss vs non-Swiss participants and across treatment arms.
empirical_analysis.dataset_and_period: Two lab experiments (March 2019 and June 2020) at the University of St. Gallen Behavioral Lab with 540 participants randomized across six treatment conditions; Swiss health-insurance institutional parameters and deductible menus for adults (CHF 300–2500) based on statutory rules and market pricing; objective health-cost distributions drawn from Swiss official statistics conditional on age and gender.
empirical_analysis.control_variables: Age; gender; disposable income category; self-rated health; expected annual health-cost belief category; self-reported risk preference; numeracy/math literacy; and session-level fixed factors as described in the experimental design.
subject: Test whether simplifying deductible choice sets or adding transparent consequence and probability information improves health-insurance deductible decisions and reduces expected welfare losses in Switzerland’s standardized mandatory health insurance market.

file.path: /mnt/data/J of Risk   Insurance - 2024 - Boonen - Pareto‐efficient risk sharing in centralized insurance markets with application to.pdf

metadata.title: Pareto-efficient risk sharing in centralized insurance markets with application to flood risk

raw_text.abstract: Centralized insurance can be found in both the private and public sectors. This paper provides a microeconomic study of the risk-sharing mechanisms in these markets, where multiple policyholders interact with a centralized monopolistic insurer. With minimal assumptions on the risk preferences of the market participants, we characterize Pareto optimality in terms of the agents' risk positions and their assessment of the likelihoods associated with their loss tail events. We relate Pareto efficiency in this market to a naturally associated cooperative game. Based on our theoretical results, we then consider a model of flood insurance coverage via an illustrative example. The lessons drawn from our theoretical results and this example lead to important policy implications for the existing National Flood Insurance Program in the United States.

sections.introduction: Develops a general theory of Pareto-efficient contracting in centralized insurance markets with multiple policyholders and a single (often monopolistic) insurer, motivated by public programs such as the U.S. National Flood Insurance Program and similar centralized catastrophe coverage settings.
sections.data: No primary dataset for estimation; provides an illustrative flood-insurance example parameterized using publicly available OpenFEMA NFIP claims data aggregated to state-month losses to create empirical states of the world for contract illustration and policy discussion.
sections.method: Models one-period risk sharing with premium vector and indemnity functions constrained to be monotone with loss to prevent ex post moral hazard; characterizes Pareto-optimal contracts via minimization of aggregate risk exposure and participation constraints; links Pareto optima to the core of an associated cooperative game and provides tail-likelihood characterizations under coherent risk measures using scenario representations and distortion-based worst-case probabilities; illustrates with multi-state flood risk pooling under a centralized insurer.
sections.results: Derives necessary and sufficient conditions for Pareto-optimal indemnities and feasible premia; shows how optimal indemnities depend on agents’ assessments of tail-event likelihoods; establishes the correspondence between coalitional stability and core allocations; in the flood example, quantifies gains from risk aggregation and geographic diversification (distant states gain more than highly correlated neighboring states) and shows how one participant’s risk appetite can affect others’ coverage in multilateral contracts.
sections.conclusion: Argues that centralized programs like NFIP could better exploit aggregation and diversification by periodic batch contracting and multilateral design, potentially increasing welfare gains and improving premium discounts relative to segregated bilateral contracting.

theoretical_summary: The paper characterizes Pareto-optimal contracts in centralized insurance markets with multiple policyholders and a single insurer by linking optimal indemnities to tail-likelihood assessments under coherent risk measures and to the core of a cooperative game, with policy lessons illustrated via a flood-risk pooling example inspired by NFIP.

file.path: /mnt/data/J of Risk   Insurance - 2024 - Born - Availability of the seat belt defense  Implications for auto liability insurance.pdf

metadata.title: Availability of the seat belt defense: Implications for auto liability insurance

raw_text.abstract: A “seat belt defense” allows a defendant in a third-party auto liability event to present evidence of seat belt nonuse to reduce a plaintiff's recovery. When successfully applied, the defense has a direct effect on reducing liability payouts by insurers for accidents. Our analysis reveals that seat belt defense laws are associated with a 10% reduction in auto claims costs, which equates to a reduction in loss costs of approximately $14 per insured vehicle. We find little evidence that the defense reduces accident frequency and no evidence that the defense affects seat belt usage. The lack of a deterrent effect on driving behavior suggests that the availability of the defense is not salient to drivers. The reduction in loss costs supports the notion that defense lawyers are aware of the defense and make use of it. The resulting effect of lowering insurance payouts may alleviate increasing auto insurance costs.
raw_text.keywords_text: automobile liability insurance; bodily injuries; seat belt defense

sections.introduction: Studies whether allowing the “seat belt defense” in third-party auto liability litigation reduces insurers’ bodily-injury payouts, claim frequency, and seat belt usage, interpreting any behavioral response as depending on the salience of the legal rule to drivers versus attorneys and adjusters.
sections.data: State-year panel for U.S. states from 1984–2014 combining seat-belt-defense legal status (statutes/case law), Insurance Research Council auto claims outcomes (bodily injury loss costs per insured car, claim frequencies, and bodily-injury-to-property-damage claim ratios), and NHTSA seat belt usage rates (with pre-1991 usage imputed), plus traffic, economic, and tort-environment controls.
sections.method: Defines treatment as an indicator for whether seat belt nonuse evidence is admissible to mitigate damages in a state-year; estimates policy effects using a staggered adoption panel design with state and year effects and an imputation-based estimator for staggered treatments; evaluates outcomes for bodily-injury loss cost, bodily-injury claim frequency, BI-to-PD ratio, and seat belt usage; assesses dynamic pre/post patterns and falsification tests.
sections.results: Finds seat-belt-defense availability is associated with about a 10% reduction in bodily injury loss costs (roughly $14 per insured vehicle) and weak or inconsistent reductions in claim frequency; finds no statistically meaningful change in seat belt usage, suggesting the defense is not salient to drivers but is utilized by defense attorneys/adjusters in settlement and litigation bargaining.
sections.conclusion: Concludes that the seat belt defense materially lowers insurer bodily-injury payouts without clear deterrence effects on driving behavior, implying a primarily legal/claims-settlement channel rather than behavioral safety improvements, with potential pass-through implications for auto insurance costs.

empirical_analysis.measuring_method_Y: State-year bodily injury (BI) loss cost defined as the average BI paid loss per insured vehicle-year including vehicles not involved in accidents (IRC data); secondary outcomes include BI claim frequency per 100 insured car-years and the BI-to-property-damage (PD) claims ratio per 100 PD claims.
empirical_analysis.measuring_method_X: Seat Belt Defense indicator equal to 1 in state-years where evidence of seat belt nonuse is admissible to mitigate damages in civil auto-liability cases, coded from state statutes and case law compilations and cross-validated with legal summaries.
empirical_analysis.methodology: Staggered-adoption state-year policy evaluation using fixed effects and an imputation-based event-study style estimator for heterogeneous treatment timing to estimate the association between seat belt defense availability and auto liability outcomes.
empirical_analysis.Robustness check method: Dynamic pre/post coefficient plots to assess pre-trends and persistence; population-weighted estimation; specifications in levels vs logs and with state-specific time trends; falsification using property-damage loss costs; placebo tests via random reassignment of enactment timing; sensitivity to alternative control-variable sets.
empirical_analysis.dataset_and_period: U.S. state-year panel, 1984–2014, combining seat belt defense law timing (legal sources), auto claims and exposure outcomes from the Insurance Research Council, seat belt usage rates from NHTSA (1991 onward with imputation for 1984–1990), and additional state-year controls from FHWA, BLS, NIAAA, IIHS, and tort-law databases.
empirical_analysis.control_variables: Primary seat belt enforcement indicator; per-capita alcohol consumption; maximum speed limit ≥70 mph indicator; rural miles share of total vehicle miles; personal income per capita; no-fault auto insurance indicator; noneconomic damages cap indicator; plus state and year fixed effects.
subject: Estimate how allowing the seat belt defense in auto-liability litigation changes insurers’ bodily-injury claim costs and claim propensity, and test whether any safety-related behavioral response occurs via higher seat belt usage.
